did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah describes the depth of the social breakdown by wishing to distance himself from the people and find an isolated place, because he sees adultery and treachery all around him.
Did you know? In this chapter, the tongue is portrayed as a weapon: the people “bend” their tongues like a bow and use them to spread lies instead of faithfulness.
Did you know? The prophet presents a reality of mutual distrust: people must be wary even of a friend and a brother, because a friend may slander and a brother may deceive.
Did you know? The Lord compares the testing of the people to refining and examining material to determine its quality, because deceit has spread among them.
Did you know? The destruction is described as complete desolation: there are no passersby, no sounds of livestock, and even the animals—from birds to cattle—have fled the land.

Did you know? Jeremiah raises a question of wisdom and understanding: Why has the land been ruined and turned into a wilderness? Later in the chapter, the answer is that the people abandoned the law, refused to listen to the Lord, and followed their own hearts and the Baals.

Did you know? In response to the disaster, the Lord commands the people to summon mourning women and skilled mourners, so they will sing a lament and awaken the people to the magnitude of the destruction.
Did you know? The chapter emphasizes that wisdom, strength, and wealth are not guarantees of deliverance, so no one should boast in these things by themselves.
Did you know? According to Jeremiah, the proper basis for boasting is knowing the Lord and understanding his ways: practicing kindness, justice, and righteousness in the land.

Did you know? The chapter concludes that an outward sign of the covenant is not enough: the house of Israel is described as “uncircumcised in heart” when the heart is not faithful to the Lord, alongside the nations judged for their uncircumcision.
